props.title: Air Doll

sections.content: Air Doll represents Hirokazu Kore-eda's haunting exploration of loneliness in modern Tokyo, following an inflatable sex doll that mysteriously comes to life. Like Blade Runner (1982) and A.I. Artificial Intelligence (2001), it probes what makes us human, but through a distinctly Japanese lens. Kore-eda's careful direction and Bae Doona's delicate performance transform what could be exploitative into a profound meditation on connection. The film shares DNA with Lars and the Real Girl (2007), though it takes a darker, more philosophical path.

sections.content: The film's visual poetry echoes similar artificial life narratives like Ex Machina (2014) and Ghost in the Shell (1995), but Kore-eda strips away sci-fi trappings for raw emotional intimacy. Cinematographer Pin Bing Lee captures Tokyo's sterile modernity alongside moments of startling tenderness. The video store setting deliberately evokes cinema's power to simulate life, while the doll's discovery of films mirrors our own journey through art seeking meaning.

Kore-eda's broader filmography, including Shoplifters (2018) and Still Walking (2008), consistently examines human connection and family bonds. Air Doll stands apart in using fantasy elements, but shares their careful observation of loneliness and desire for belonging. The film's treatment of artificial life connects to earlier works like Metropolis (1927) and later ones like After Yang (2021), though with distinctly Japanese cultural elements around objects potentially containing souls. sections.content: Through its artificial protagonist, Air Doll examines contemporary Japanese attitudes toward sexuality, commodification, and authentic existence. Like Ghost in the Shell (1995) and Paprika (2006), it uses the artificial body as a lens to examine identity. The doll's experiences working in the video store and discovering cinema mirror Japan's post-war relationship with Western culture, while her physical fragility speaks to broader themes of human impermanence.
